articles.text: Kolhapur: The Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union, popularly known as Gokul Milk Union, has decided to increase the selling price of buffalo milk by Rs 6 per litre and cow milk by Rs 4 per litre with immediate effect, its chairman Rajesh Patil said on Saturday.The decision was taken unanimously by all 25 directors due to the drought situation and the difficulties faced by farmers, Patil, a former MLA, said.The union has also decided to raise the procurement rates paid to milk producers by Rs 3 per litre for buffalo milk and Rs 2 per litre for cow milk, he said, adding that this hike was "historic".Also Read | Milk prices rise despite winter flush, and more pain may lie ahead"The revised rates will come into effect from November 21 and remain applicable for around 131 days, till March. A dairy farm requires three to four bags every day. The additional amount should have been given directly to farmers, he added.Drought and lack of rainfall had added to difficulties, while the cost of maintaining cattle sheds had become unaffordable, he claimed."The increase has largely benefited the union rather than milk producers," the farmer alleged.Rajesh Patil, backed by the ruling Mahayuti, was elected chairman of the Gokul Milk Union after defeating Shashikant Patil-Chuyekar of the Samvichari Aghadi by 16 votes to 13 in a keenly contested election held in November.

articles.title: India And France Discuss Ways To Counter Terror Financing And Online Radicalisation
articles.text:
India and France held the 18th meeting of the Joint Working Group (JWG) on Counter Terrorism (CT) in New Delhi on Friday, exchanging views on the threat of terrorism in their respective regions and globally, including state-sponsored and cross-border terrorism.
According to the Ministry of External Affairs ( MEA), both sides unequivocally condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including cross-border terrorism and violent extremism. They also reiterated their strong condemnation of the April 2025 heinous Pahalgam terrorist attack and the November 2025 terror incident near Red Fort in New Delhi.
The meeting was co-chaired by Suhel Ajaz Khan, Additional Secretary (CT) at the MEA, and Olivier Caron, French Ambassador at large and Special Envoy for Counter-Terrorism and Organised Crime.
“Both sides also discussed addressing the traditional and emerging challenges to counter terrorism, including the threats posed by the misuse of new and emerging technologies and financial technologies by terrorists and terrorist groups. The Indian side also briefed on the comprehensive National Counter Terrorism Policy and Strategy – Prahaar,” the MEA stated.
“The two sides discussed strengthening bilateral cooperation, including cooperation in countering financing of terrorism and online radicalisation, information sharing, capacity-building and training, and sharing of experiences and best practices,” it added.
India and France also reaffirmed their commitment to enhancing cooperation in the multilateral forums, including the United Nations, Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and No Money for Terror (NMFT).
The two sides agreed to hold the 19th meeting of the Joint Working Group in France on a mutually convenient date, the MEA mentioned.
Last week, India and France reviewed progress in their bilateral space cooperation, including between ISRO and CNES, and discussed pathways to facilitate commercial space collaboration between the two countries’ space industrial ecosystems at the 3rd India-France Strategic Space Dialogue in Paris.
“Foreign Secretary Shri Vikram Misri, along with Secretary General of the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Martin Briens, co-chaired the 3rd India-France Strategic Space Dialogue earlier today in Paris,” the MEA posted on X.
The two sides reviewed the ongoing space cooperation and discussed ways to further strengthen it.
“Reviewed progress in the wide-ranging ongoing bilateral space cooperation, including between ISRO and CNES. Discussed avenues for furthering strategic space cooperation and pathways to facilitate commercial space collaboration between the two space industrial ecosystems. Exchanged views on multilateral space matters,” the MEA said.
(IANS)

articles.title: U.S. Navy Prepares for Third Zumwalt Hypersonic Upgrade
articles.text:
The U.S. Navy is preparing to begin a more than two-year overhaul of USS Michael Monsoor in 2028 as the third Zumwalt-class destroyer to receive the service’s new Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missile system.

The U.S. Navy is seeking industry input ahead of a major overhaul of its second Zumwalt-class guided-missile destroyer, USS Michael Monsoor (DDG-1001), that will equip the stealth warship with new long-range hypersonic missiles and overhaul several of its onboard combat and engineering systems. Michael Monsoor‘s modernization follows the start of CPS depot modernizations to USS Zumwalt (DDG-1000) and USS Lyndon B. Johnson (DDG-1002).

The Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA) announced Nov. 17 that it will host an industry day in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 9 to assess shipyard capabilities and technical requirements for the destroyer’s upcoming Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) Depot Modernization Period (DMP), scheduled to begin in May 2028 and conclude in August 2030.

According to NAVSEA, the 27-month modernization effort will require “large-scale structural modifications” and compartment reconfiguration (mirroring previous CPS conversions) to accommodate the new CPS payload modules and launch infrastructure, alongside upgrades to the destroyer’s combat systems, computing architecture, electrical distribution, and cooling equipment.

The service is replacing each ship’s 155mm Advanced Gun Systems with large-diameter vertical launch tubes designed to accommodate the joint service CPS missiles, which Naval News previously reported are slated for future storage at Naval Weapons Station Yorktown.

The Navy is also planning a comprehensive modernization of the ship’s Total Ship Computing Environment (TSCE), including new hardware and software, open-architecture improvements, and interfaces needed to integrate the hypersonic weapon into the destroyer’s existing combat systems.

Additional modifications will focus on expanding the ship’s electrical and thermal management capacity, including improvements to power conversion and distribution systems and high-efficiency chilled-water cooling equipment.

The announcement provides one of the clearest publicly disclosed schedules yet for the second Zumwalt-class destroyer’s hypersonic conversion, establishing a May 2028 start date and August 2030 completion target for the work.

Once complete in 2030, the service will have a trio of CPS-armed destroyers, which it plans to relocate to Pearl Harbor alongside a number of guided missile submarines over the next several years as a modern “Battleship Row”.

articles.title: J&K Police intensifies crackdown on terror networks, attaches 122 properties in 2026
articles.text:
Jammu and Kashmir Director General of Police Nalin Prabhat on Wednesday said local terrorist recruitment in the Union Territory had been brought down to “almost zero” over the past two years.
Only two Kashmiri youths joined the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) during this period. The last remaining terrorist among them, identified as Lateef Bhat, was killed in an encounter in Kulgam district on Wednesday. The other terrorist, Umar Nisar, was eliminated in the same district two days ago, he said.
The DGP was speaking at the passing-out parade of deputy superintendents of police, sub-inspectors and assistant directors of the Forest Protection Force at the Sher-i-Kashmir Police Academy (SKPA) in the presence of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha in Udhampur.
“We have brought local terrorist recruitment in Jammu and Kashmir to almost zero over the last two years. During this period, only two Kashmiri youths joined the Lashkar-e-Taiba,” Prabhat said.
“Today, I would like to inform everyone that the last remaining terrorist, Lateef Bhat, was killed in Kulgam today. Two days earlier, Umar Nisar was also killed in Kulgam,” he said.
The DGP said the Jammu and Kashmir Police had been fighting Pakistan-sponsored terrorism for the past 35 years and paid tributes to its martyrs.
“We have been fighting Pakistan-sponsored terrorism for the last 35 years. I pay my tributes and salute our 1,603 martyrs, including our two brave personnel, Babi Chand and Rashpal Kumar, who laid down their lives for the nation in Kishtwar recently,” he said.
“Their supreme sacrifices make us stronger and further strengthen our resolve. The memories of our martyrs always show us the way, remaining our guiding light and source of inspiration,” he said.
The DGP said the police force was not only fighting terrorists but also targeting their support networks and the broader terror ecosystem.
“I am extremely grateful to our Hon’ble Prime Minister, our Hon’ble Home Minister and, particularly, our respected Lieutenant Governor, Manoj Sinha Ji, under whose guidance and leadership the Jammu and Kashmir Police is continuously achieving one success after another and hoisting its flag of victory everywhere.
“We are not only combating terrorism but are also continuously striking at its ecosystem. Our endeavour is to completely dismantle and destroy the entire terror ecosystem,” he said.
Giving details of the action against terror-related networks, the DGP said 240 accused were arrested under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in 2025, while 210 arrests had been made under the stringent law this year.
The arrests included those of people allegedly providing financial and logistical support to terrorist activities, he said, adding that those involved in such activities would not escape the police’s reach.
On action against properties linked to terrorism, Prabhat said 155 properties were attached in 2025 after due legal process, while 122 had been attached so far this year.
He said the action covered properties belonging to terrorists operating from Pakistan, as well as those of other individuals involved in terrorism-related activities under the UAPA.
Top Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Lateef Bhat was killed in an encounter with security forces in Kulgam district on Wednesday, officials said.
Bhat, along with another terrorist, Umar Nisar, was involved in the November 11 attack on CRPF personnel in Kulgam, which left three paramilitary personnel injured. Nisar was killed in an encounter in Kulgam on Monday.

IAF Seeks 500 Expendable ISR Drones, Invites Indian Vendors to Submit Responses
articles.text:
Indian drone manufacturers, defence startups and OEMs will have an opportunity to supply 500 Expendable Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) following a Request for Information (RFI) from the Indian Air Force (IAF).
The RFI, referenced RFI_EISRUAS_ASR_IAF_18NOV26, was published on 18 th November 2026 by the Directorate of Plans, Air Headquarters, Vayu Bhawan, Rafi Marg, New Delhi. A response should be returned by 12 th January 2027 at 5pm. The RFI is open to local suppliers and OEMs to provide 500 expendable ISR drones. It is intended to support local industry, and relaxations for startups and Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE’s) apply in line with the conditions outlined. There is no tender fee or Earnest Money Deposit (EMD).
The IAF is seeking to increase the number of Unmanned Systems in its inventory for Intelligence and Surveillance operations. Expendable UAVs can be used in situations where recovery is not possible. Expendable systems may have a different role to recoverable surveillance systems, particularly in theatre environments.
These systems may be used to perform reconnaissance, monitoring enemy positions, monitoring activity within operational areas, and gathering information with reduced risk to manned platforms and crews.
Opportunities for Indian industry
This RFI provides opportunities for local businesses to supply small Unmanned Air Systems, ISR payload systems, navigation systems and ancillary systems. With relaxations for startups and MSEs in place, this opportunity may allow a greater variety of businesses to enter, providing they meet the conditions outlined in the tender documents.
For local manufacturers, this requirement presents opportunities throughout the supply chain such as airframe, propulsion, battery, Electro Optic and Infra Red sensors, communication systems, ground control systems and mission planning.
However, without reviewing the full details of the RFI document it cannot be confirmed what technical specification the aircraft will have. In order to fully understand the aircraft’s requirements such as endurance, range, payload capacity, launch/recovery system, communications and sensor capabilities, further consideration is required of the full RFI document.

articles.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
articles.text:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.

The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.

You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks. Great to be here.

I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.

I know.

It’s like a normal thing that happened.

It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.

[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.

Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.

Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”

What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?

I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.

But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.

I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.

So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.

Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?

Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.

Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.

Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.

I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.

Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?

They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.

But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.

I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.

But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.

I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.

I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.

That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.

That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?

I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.

This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.

The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.

They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.

What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s big business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways.

If you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that big enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet.

That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much.

I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time.

The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model.

So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.”

So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting.

I actually heard Nadella this week say every company will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does.

The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things.

I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap.

Yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out.

Exactly.

It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders?

Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with.

Let’s talk about the governance issues. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history.

If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model.

Anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public company, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety.

Yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this. It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more.

But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial, Sam Altman famously says, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times.

Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT.

I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them said that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot.

Ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed. They could say, “Oh look, don’t release this model. It’s too dangerous.” The trust doesn’t have any of those powers. All it can do is appoint or remove certain board members. Even then, they have to give 30 days’ notice to a small committee of the board, which includes Daniela Amodei, the chair of that little committee who is also a founder of Anthropic.

To oversimplify things, out of these seven board seats, the trust gets to pick three, the founders get to pick three, and then the kind of tie-breaking seat, the seventh one, the trust technically appoints, but they have to basically get founder approval to do it. So it’s one of these things that’s so complex, but when you really look at the nitty-gritty of it, the founders have pretty unchecked control here. I think that’s something that’s getting lost in the narrative of, “Oh, this trust is above us. Don’t worry.” Okay, well, they don’t really have much power to check you.

The founder control structure is the wildest thing I have ever read about in years of doing the show and thinking about business. Anthropic has seven founders. They have been issued a single share of stock that holds 50.1 percent of the voting power of the company. That is issued to a company called Founder LLC, and they’re the seven co-owners of Founder LLC.

How on earth does that work? Do they just all get together and then decide how to vote the one share of stock?

Yeah, it’s really interesting and that’s why I was kind of oversimplifying it a minute ago with who gets to choose this tie-breaking seat because it’s technically Founder LLC. It’s just a total mess. But when you really look at the simplified version, it’s that yes, through all of these weird structures and things they’ve done, they basically have pretty unchecked power and that’s the way they want it.

When I was talking to a former employee who recently left, they said it’s not necessarily that the founders have a financial interest in making the most money. In their eyes, it’s more that they have an interest in unchecked control. I think that’s a really important point here.

Some dissenters within the ranks of Anthropic think it’s not about them wanting to get rich, but rather it’s about them wanting that total control, which does track with a lot of their public statements. They say, “You can’t do safety from second place.” They’re all in on speeding up this race, but the problem is when you speed up the AI race, you’re speeding it up for everyone involved.

The safety piece is the really interesting portion of this to me because it’s the thing you would spend money on, absent some huge litigation drama or liability concern, that no other company would spend money on.

So let’s say it’s proven in court that model companies are liable for what people’s agents do. I think then all the model companies would build safety systems. They would have some big incentive to make sure their models are safe. That has not yet happened. We don’t know. There’s a big debate about safety and where the regulation will come from and what will create the incentives.

In the meantime, you’ve got seven founders holding a single share of stock who right now appear to be aligned on investing in safety in various ways inside of Anthropic. What happens if they start to disagree?

Yeah, that’s a great question. I think that the other interesting question here is what happens when you can explain away anything in the name of safety if you’re thinking it’s “for the greater good,” which as we know is a common villain trope in every movie. But it’s also one of Anthropic’s main things on its website. They’re like, “We want to do this for the greater good, for the global good.”

If you’re saying, “Hey, we have to win this race at all costs because we’re the only good guys and anyone else who wins it is going to do worse than us,” are you really the good guy at that point? And can’t you just explain away any single decision, even dropping some safety measures, as saying, “Oh, it’s slowing us down too much. We’re going to lose. We’ve got to win at all costs”? So you drop this or drop that. And then you look in the mirror at the end of the race and you say, “Oh, actually, we’re the exact same as the other company we’re trying to be different from.” I think that’s increasingly happening.

So I mean, right now they’ve said, “Look, we’re really committed to this.” You do have to remember that these people are almost religiously dedicated to this idea of safe AI. A lot of them think that AI systems are potentially conscious. I mean, this is by Anthropic founders’ own statements.

So I think that it’s not like they’re just secretly only trying to make money and just talking about safety and they don’t mean it. I think it’s more something a little more dangerous in that they want complete control because they believe that they have the right plan for AI safety and they will do it better than anyone else.

But as we know, absolute power corrupts absolutely. So a lot of Anthropic employees that I was talking to, former ones, were saying, “Yeah, it does not make sense that this industry is so unregulated. There’s no external regulation. Even if these seven people think they have the best idea for AI safety, okay, then prove it to someone else — that you shouldn’t be the only ones deciding this. Because you’re not elected.” So that’s the consensus among some.

They have a morally binding handshake agreement to allow external auditors, Hayden. It’s going to be fine.

Oh, yeah, with employee-level access.

Also, it’s called “Super Intelligence” now. It’s going to be totally fine. They all went to the White House and they looked deeply into each other’s eyes and said it was going to be fine.

Obviously Anthropic came up with this structure well before the events with Nvidia and Jensen Huang, but I can’t help but put them together in my head. They are happening at the same time. And Nvidia has a very traditional corporate governance structure.

Jensen owned 3 percent of the company, but he had a board of directors. The board of directors determined that he had violated the company’s code of conduct in some way. He resigned. It’s very obvious that he was thoroughly encouraged to resign, but that’s just normal corporate governance. That’s what you learn about in school. A company has a board of directors. Their number one job is to hire and fire the CEO.

That’s very different in Silicon Valley, right? Founder control of companies is a big story everywhere. Mark Zuckerberg famously has control over Meta, even though Meta shareholders repeatedly vote to remove him, which is one of the underemphasized stories in all of American business. Sergey Brin and Larry Page control Google.

Is this more in the, “We need to insulate our founders from the demands of the market and boards of directors” in classic Silicon Valley style? Or is it, “We need to insulate our founders and Dario from the demands of the market so we can stay focused on AGI and safety”? Because it feels like a combination of both.

It’s definitely a combination. I mean, they say it’s the latter. I think in a lot of ways it’s like the former. It’s totally a combination. I’d say it’s about 50/50. I mean, they want control so that they can focus on what they think is best and not lose control to someone that they don’t think knows best. But ironically, as we know, no one group of people should be in control of what is best here. So at least that’s what a lot of my sources say.

So I think that, yeah, I mean, it’s just a combination. Elon Musk famously won’t run a company that he doesn’t have voting control over. So I think it’s just a new Valley thing and it’s pervading here for a couple of different reasons.

There are seven of them. What seven different people do over the course of the next five to 10 years is as unpredictable as anything. What happens if one of them does something illegal or lies to the board or smuggles chips to China or anything? Is there some way to remove one of these founders from this LLC?

Yeah. I mean, allegedly the trust has the power to remove. They haven’t said whether they have the power to remove all of the board or just some, but in some way when you’re looking at the fine print of the S-1, basically if the trust gives 30 days’ notice to essentially Daniela Amodei and her other two people on this subcommittee, then they can suggest removal of a board member. Again, they can waive that 30-day notice if they deem it correct, if Daniela does.

But yeah, there’s a lot of fine print here. Essentially, yes, you can remove someone and there is stuff about that in the S-1 saying if they’ve done something illegal, if they’ve done something really bad, they can be removed, but it’s definitely not easy. It also depends on who it is, I think.

It’s interesting. I keep coming back to this because it is so complicated, it’s so unusual, and it is right next to the Nvidia situation where he materially misrepresented his relationship to the shareholders by having his PR people issue statements saying it was all normal. He had to admit that it wasn’t all normal and he was in fact involved in extramarital affairs and the board fired him.

I felt a little bad for that PR guy who had to put his name on all those statements that ended up being a lie.

I feel nothing. As the audience may know, as Hayden is well aware, we make all the PR people put their names on everything just in case something like this happens. That’s just a little bit of Verge trivia.

Anyhow, right, I mean, that’s just normal governance. Here you have a company where the only check might be the market itself, right?

Yep.

If they can’t sell tokens for more than what they make them for, they’re going to have to report that in the financials and the market might say this company is failing and pull all the money back. That is a very different kind of pressure.

If the only meaningful way that Dario might lose his job is if the company goes bankrupt and then the swirl of things is he’s got to buy chips before OpenAI can buy the chips, he’s got to increase the number of verticals that Anthropic competes in within the enterprise, and he also idealistically has to train the next model and the next model with RSI to get to AGI, it feels like actually the pressure is to go as fast as possible. If I just added that up, I would say I would not slow down ever.

Yeah. That’s why I say you can kind of explain away anything if you’re trying to be first, which they are. And they’ve been very public about that. Regarding the money thing, Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School, told me this week that the trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power and that you either trust that they’re going to balance the interest of society appropriately or you don’t.

But either way, the real constraint on whatever impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money. That’s the thing, Anthropic needs money. In a livestream recently, Dario told the CEO of JPMorgan Chase that compute is the “deepest business dilemma” that the company faces. Essentially if you buy too much, you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers.

Even more importantly, you can’t do the R&D. You can’t come up with new models. So they’re extremely compute-constrained, even maybe more so than OpenAI because OpenAI was made fun of for a long time for losing a ton of money, but they were investing a lot in compute. Anthropic did not do that as much, and now they’re having to pay the piper.

So it’s an interesting turnaround here. Hopefully for them and their interests, I guess, if they can get the compute they need. But as we know, the supply is a lot lower than the demand. So it’s just going to be interesting to see what they will do to make money and therefore money to buy compute.

It’s funny. A couple of weeks ago I told our colleague, Liz Lopatto, that the Anthropic IPO would be one of the biggest stories of the year. She was laughing at me today, because she says it’s not even the biggest story of the week because of Jensen Huang and Nvidia.

My argument — take it or leave it, and you can judge whether I’m correct — is that they are the same story. That if Nvidia’s financing architecture fails or wobbles because Jensen isn’t there to bully everyone into believing in it, then maybe you do have a glut of chips sitting in data centers without the appropriate permitting or power to light them up and the market for chips will change dramatically.

Maybe a company like CoreWeave does get way more wobbly or some of the already wobbly neoclouds start to get wobbly and the price of compute falls and lets Anthropic compete differently. Maybe a bunch of chips that were allocated to China on the gray market come flooding back to the United States.

That apparently will happen.

Right? So there’s a lot of ways the Nvidia story affects Anthropic’s financials. Has the company said anything about that yet? Is the market reacting to that in any way?

Not yet. They’ve just talked about how important compute is and that it’s going to be a really big issue for them. And Anthropic’s IPO, it has a lot of ties to Nvidia and there’s a lot of complexities here because Nvidia had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement on top of a $10 billion funding promise it made last year.

So they are in bed together, and that’s going to be interesting to see, too. The new CEO of Nvidia has made a lot of claims about diverting chips that were potentially going to China and bringing them back so they’re not doing that anymore.

Now we’re going to see if there’s more supply or not. Also, Jensen personally made some of these deals, especially with large financial institutions to fund the AI infrastructure buildout last August. So he’s wheeling and dealing a lot. And so it’s going to remain to be seen whether the new chief executive has that kind of power to wheel and deal and pressure people into doing stuff like this or not.

This is my last question. Obviously everyone’s just celebrating today. We are probably throwing the most cold water on this by noting that the structure of Anthropic is very odd. What should people be looking for? What are the signs that you’re looking for now that Anthropic is a stock that’s trading? What’s the relationship in your mind between the value of Anthropic stock on any given day and the broader AI story?

I think that stock is a little bit like benchmarks in the AI industry in that sometimes it doesn’t mean what you think it means and also it never means everything. So you always take it with a grain of salt. It’s all vibes based. It’s all hype. So people get scared, they sell, and people hear one good thing or a rumor and they buy. So I think it’s important to look at it and see what’s driving that fear or hype that day or that week. But it’s also really important to see what the company says in these reports and earnings calls.

That’s what I think is the most interesting. Not really the numbers all the time, but instead, what they try to sneak into these reports by saying, “Oh, we sidelined this team,” or, “We discontinued this safety initiative all in the name of being first.”

That’s the type of thing that I think we’re going to see a lot of and that’s what I want to watch for. Because the company that made its bed on safe AI is increasingly looking the same as OpenAI and is going to have a lot of swept-under-the-rug type of updates like that, if my sources are right.

You heard it here first. Former CNBC reporter Hayden Field says, look past the day-to-day swings into the fundamentals of the company. That’s good. Also, the stock market is only vibes. That’s the other thing I heard you say.

Yep. I mean, it’s controversial, but after being a financial reporter, yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of vibes there. It’s a lot of vibes.

Oh, I agree. I think sometimes the only thing they ask me to go on CNBC to say is this is just vibes, and then they usher me off the air very quickly.

Hayden, this is great. We’re obviously going to be talking about this story many times with you in the year to come. Hopefully we can do another straightforward business story and not just a soap opera one.

I’ll be here for both. We’ve got to do them both.

Amazing. Thank you so much, Hayden.

Thanks.

articles.title: IG Defence Qualifies 2.5 kg Anti-Personnel Warhead in Indian Army Trials Recommended
articles.text:
Indian defence technology company IG Defence has announced that its indigenously designed 2.5 kg anti-personnel warhead has successfully qualified in Indian Army trials after being integrated with the VALARI 1.5 OFC platform.
The company announced the development through a LinkedIn post, describing the warhead as a proprietary design developed in India. The announcement marks a reported trial milestone for IG Defence’s efforts to develop indigenous payloads for unmanned aerial strike systems.
The warhead was evaluated as part of the VALARI 1.5 OFC platform, indicating its intended integration with an optical-fibre-controlled unmanned aerial vehicle. Fibre-optic control is increasingly relevant to battlefield drones because it can provide a communication link that is less vulnerable to conventional radio-frequency jamming.
Optical Fibre FPVs allow control and video data to be transmitted via an actual cable to be carried with the aircraft. This helps provide control in EW scenarios where RF communication would be compromised.
IG Defence have developed optical fibre FPVs. Their publically available FPV OFC system provides precise strike and reconnaissance capabilities in electrically contested environments. The system uses up to 10km of optical fibre and has an endurance of up to 50 minutes. It is unclear whether the VALARI 1.5 OFC constitutes a variant of this system, or a separate system configuration.
This development follows increased interest from the Indian Army in optical fibre controlled FPV suicide drones. In November 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs released draft RFP information for optical fibre and RF controlled FPV suicide aerial vehicles. The information states day/night versions of the system will be provided, with ground control stations and HE AP warheads. The system must be able to perform missions beyond 15km, including a minimum 7.5km optical fibre section with RF control. Two HE AP warheads must be delivered, with a 10m lethality range.
These are draft requirements for procurement and should not be confused with the specification or performance data of the 2.5kg warhead in IG Defence’s systems. IG Defence have been increasing their range of UAS, with FPV strike drones, Optical Fibre controlled systems, surveillance UAS and counter-drone systems. With this latest announcement, the company can now report that this system qualifies for trials with the Indian Army, with an indigenous warhead.

articles.title: India, Canada conclude sixth round of talks for proposed trade pact
articles.text:
India and Canada have concluded the sixth round of negotiations for a trade agreement, aimed at unlocking new opportunities in trade and investment, and diversifying supply chains, an official statement said on Saturday.
The negotiations covered key areas, including trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, trade remedies, intellectual property and investment promotion, the commerce ministry said.
Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal held a meeting with Glenn Purves, Vice Minister of International Trade of Canada, and his delegation to review the progress of negotiations for the proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
The ten-day talks concluded on November 20.
"Both sides reaffirmed their shared commitment to concluding an ambitious, balanced and commercially meaningful agreement that delivers tangible benefits to farmers, industries, businesses and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in both countries," it said.

articles.title: Philippines Weighs Pinaka as Cheaper Alternative to HIMARS and Chunmoo
articles.text:
The Pinaka rocket system is being considered by the Philippines as a more affordable alternative compared to the K239 Chunmoo (South Korea) and HIMARS (USA). Therefore, it may be the correct choice for the Philippine Army.
It may be that the Philippines will choose different systems for its army and marines. The Pinaka may be chosen for the Philippine Army whereas the HIMARS may be purchased by the Philippine Marine Corps. There is currently no official confirmation of any decisions by the Government or purchases made.
Price considerations
Multiple rocket launchers vary greatly depending on various factors such as what launcher they have, the type of ammunition, range and support required, and how many systems are included. Therefore, if Pinaka is cheaper it may be an appealing option. However, the true total cost will depend on what type of rocket is used, training required, maintenance costs and future supply options.
Pinaka has been developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation of India, and manufactured by domestic defence companies. Currently, it is in active service within the Indian Army. As India is looking to export more indigenous weapons, the Pinaka has gained interest. Due to increasing expansion and modernisation of the Philippines armed forces, there has been interest in obtaining systems which provide ground based firepower.
HIMARS and K239 Chunmoo are also in contention. The HIMARS has been heavily used and has high demand internationally. The K239 Chunmoo provides a different launcher and ammunition combination. When considering these systems in the Philippines, consideration must be given to the specific operational requirements of the military. Range, mobility, availability of ammunition and compatibility with current forces must all be considered.
Although it is suggested that Pinaka will be chosen for the army and HIMARS for the marines, this is currently only a suggestion. There is currently no official confirmation from the Philippines that they will purchase either the Pinaka, HIMARS or K239 Chunmoo. Until an official statement is released from Manila, it should be considered that these choices (and the potential division) are merely potential options.

articles.title: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it
articles.text:
My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?"

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.

But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?"

Easy: it did.

Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.

But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.

A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.

Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture, so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.

The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.

Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?

("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud?" "Do as I say, not as I do.")

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.

If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®

articles.title: Chinese-Character Usernames Edits Put India’s Digital Mapping Strategy in Focus
articles.text:
Multiple changes have been made to data related to India’s borders within mapping platforms in the past 30 days. This highlights a concern in ensuring that representations of India’s borders and associated features in globally popular mapping platforms are monitored properly.
Changes to data have been made in locations along India’s borders, as indicated by the maps below. The usernames of contributors to these edits are represented in Chinese characters. One of these locations has been highlighted by an open source intelligence account (@detresfa_) on social media. This has raised concerns as to whether these changes are one-off events or part of a larger pattern which may require further investigation.
The presence of Chinese characters in the usernames of the contributors does not necessarily indicate the nationality, location or intention of the editor(s). Additionally, changes to data on open mapping platforms do not necessarily imply changes to internationally recognised borders. A detailed investigation into the version history, location and underlying data of these changes must be conducted in order to understand the intentions behind them.
Broader concerns:
As open mapping platforms are often utilised as sources of geographic data by developers, researchers, business uses and organisations, changes made to commonly re-used data in these platforms can affect representations of geographic features and boundaries in many subsequent applications.
Importance of multiple changes to maps
Within OpenStreetMap (OSM) in particular, it is important to monitor changes to data, as anyone can make changes to data to improve accuracy. However, this means changes to data in sensitive geographic areas must be carefully monitored.
Contested borders are handled in OpenStreetMap according to a policy set out in the OpenStreetMap Foundation. In order to represent real-world conditions, contested borders in OSM are not adjusted to match the preferred borders of any given country. As such, contested borders present a sensitive issue in terms of both technical and political aspects.
Whilst inaccuracies in representations of a country in one mapping platform do not automatically lead to inaccuracies in all global mapping databases, or define the legal borders of a country, if this data is used as a reference by other services, inaccuracies may be replicated in different digital products. Therefore, it is important that inaccuracies are identified quickly, documented and corrected.
In relation to India, it is critical that issues like this do not only be addressed once inaccuracies in mapping data have spread. To help prevent this, a system should be put in place to continuously monitor changes in geographic features and border-related data in sensitive border areas. Furthermore, previous versions of data should be documented and appropriate technical amendments made quickly via platform channels.
Encouraging global use of Survey of India data
There is a strong foundation in place within India to address this issue through the Survey of India (SoI). SoI is the national mapping agency under the Department of Science and Technology.
Within the Online Maps Portal, a variety of digital mapping data is available. This includes administrative boundary data, village boundary data, vector data, georeferenced raster maps and topographical data. According to the frequently asked questions within this portal, administrative boundary data and village boundary data are freely available to all users. Other products may have conditions of registration or payment.
According to the geospatial data guidelines published by the government in 2021, Survey of India maps and boundary data should form the standard for political maps of India at all levels (national, state and others). These datasets should be freely available for easy download, and can be viewed in digital format, or printed.
Therefore, it is not so much a problem that authoritative mapping data does not exist in India, but rather that it is easier to locate, access and utilise within the global geospatial data community.
India should encourage international mapping platforms, software developers, academic institutions and geospatial businesses to utilise its authoritative vector boundary data. If data is made available in a machine readable format using stable APIs, well documented, regularly updated and easily licensed, software developers will find it easy to include official Indian datasets in their applications.
Considering creation of global basemap
As an even more ambitious option, India could create a free, reliable global basemap (raster based) using authoritative vector data. This would allow India to contribute to the global mapping data community, rather than being heavily reliant on mapping data from overseas platforms.
This does not necessarily mean political changes to global maps. If a credible global basemap is created from an Indian perspective, it should follow clear technical standards. International borders should be clearly separated from contested claims, source information should be clearly documented, and methodology should be publicly available. Its value comes from reliability, consistency and providing another authoritative source.
By creating a global basemap from India, domestic geospatial businesses, research institutions, navigation applications and government services may benefit. Developers will have a reliable source of geographic data, and India’s mapping capabilities will gain increased international recognition.
To successfully achieve this, continuous investment would be required in maintaining data, having consistent mapping standards, cloud infrastructure, open APIs and forming relationships with other members of the global geospatial community. Basemaps must be regularly updated, and there must be a transparent process in place to fix errors and include validated data.

articles.title: KSSL Showcases Israeli ROCKS Missile in Portfolio, Points to Local Production
articles.text:
KSSL have highlighted inclusion of the Israeli ‘ROCKS’ (Crystal Maze II) missile in their missile portfolio. However, further details on the production arrangement, timeframes and extent of local content in this system have yet to be provided by KSSL.
ROCKS is an air launched standoff missile developed by Rafael Advanced Defence Systems of Israel. Inclusion of ROCKS into KSSL’s missile portfolio indicates that KSSL are seeking to offer this system to meet requirements within the Indian defence sector.
Significance
If production of ROCKS is to take place within India, it supports increased indigenous production within the sector as targeted by government policy. It also indicates involvement of local industry in supplying this product. However, it is currently unclear what level of involvement local industry would have in production of this product. It is unknown if ROCKS would be locally assembled, produced under licence or with greater technology transfer.
Context
The inclusion of this air launched standoff missile follows an increase in capability within India’s combat aircraft. Air launched standoff weapons provide combat aircraft with increased flexibility in engaging protected targets. However, this inclusion does not indicate that a contract has been signed, nor that the missile has been ordered by the Indian Air Force or integrated onto any specific aircraft.
Uncertainties
Uncertainties remain regarding when production may start within India, or which sites and partners will be involved. Furthermore, understanding just how much of this missile will be produced within India will be important to understand the extent of local content.
Conclusion
Overall, the inclusion of ROCKS within KSSL’s missile portfolio demonstrates KSSL’s interest in importing this Israeli missile to meet requirements within India. However, further information on production and the current status of the programme will be required.

articles.text: In a market where investors are often drawn to hot themes, hypergrowth stocks and the prospect of multibagger returns, PPFAS Mutual Fund CIO and Director Rajeev Thakkar reiterates the importance of staying focused on fundamentals rather than chasing popular investment trends.During its 13th Unitholders’ Meet on Saturday, Thakkar explained why PPFAS does not actively chase companies expected to become 10-baggers, 20-baggers or even 100-baggers. He said the fund house's investment decisions are guided by the quality of a business, its financial performance and the valuation at which it is available rather than the excitement surrounding a particular sector or investment theme.<blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">CIO @RajeevThakkar reiterates why we steer clear of "hot themes" and stick to fundamentals.#PPFASAGM https://t.co/5JkZYQkyGC</p>— PPFAS (@PPFAS) <a href="https://x.com/PPFAS/status/2124100106819654140?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 21, 2026</a></blockquote><script async="" src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script>Also Read | Capitalmind Flexi Cap Fund increases stake in MCX, Radico Khaitan, 9 others, makes exit from Bajaj Auto and 8 moreTo illustrate his point, Thakkar compared Coal India, which is part of the fund house's portfolio, with a popular company operating in a hot investment theme that PPFAS Mutual Fund does not own. He clarified that the comparison was not intended to criticise the other company but to demonstrate why the price investors pay for growth matters.Coal India reported revenue of Rs 1.71 lakh crore and profits of over Rs 33,000 crore, compared with Rs 78,000 crore in revenue and less than Rs 500 crore in profits for the other company. While Coal India offered a 6.6% dividend yield and traded at a PE of around 7, the other company paid no dividends and traded at a PE of over 700.Thakkar acknowledged that the hot-theme company could grow its business and profits in the coming years. However, he questioned how long it could take for a company earning less than Rs 500 crore to reach the profit levels of a business already generating more than Rs 33,000 crore.Thakkar also cited examples of past investment themes to explain why investors should be careful about paying excessive valuations for companies with strong growth prospects.He referred to a company that had tripled its profits over five years, but whose stock price had declined by around one-third. The reason, he explained, was that the starting valuation was too high and investors had built in expectations of substantial future growth.Despite the sharp correction and the threefold increase in profits, the stock was still trading at a PE multiple of more than 70. This illustrated why even a well-managed company with promising business prospects may not necessarily turn out to be a good investment if investors pay too much for it.Thakkar also challenged the notion that investors should always prefer companies with high earnings growth.He explained that even a company with zero earnings growth could be an attractive investment if it generated cash flows equivalent to its earnings and distributed all its profits to shareholders as dividends.Using a theoretical example, he said a stock trading at five times its earnings and distributing all its profits as dividends would offer a 20% dividend yield. Even if its earnings remained unchanged for 25 years, he would be comfortable owning such a business because of the cash flows it generated for shareholders.He said investment decisions should not be based solely on earnings multiples or growth rates. Investors need to consider both the growth potential of a business and whether they are paying a reasonable valuation for it.Thakkar said there are several misconceptions about what equity fund managers should and should not do. He clarified that the investment team does not attempt to predict quarterly earnings surprises, changes in interest rates, foreign portfolio investor (FPI) flows, geopolitical developments or the outcome of political events. These factors can influence stock prices but are largely outside the control of fund managers.Thakkar also addressed investor concerns about artificial intelligence (AI), the capital expenditure cycle and the sustainability of investments made by global technology companies.He acknowledged that AI is a significant technological development and could create substantial opportunities. However, he also cautioned that excessive capital expenditure in the sector could lead to disruptions over the next two to three years.Also Read | Silver ETFs crash over 56% from January peak. Should investors buy, hold or exit?Thakkar also pointed out that the availability of open-source and open-weight AI models could change the competitive landscape. While these models may not match the most advanced frontier models in every aspect, they could be sufficient for several everyday business applications.Therefore, the fund house believes that investing in companies with multiple established revenue streams can offer a different risk profile compared with businesses whose success depends largely on a single AI model or emerging business.Thakkar also addressed concerns about the fund house's investments in Indian IT services companies, including TCS, Infosys and HCL Technologies. He clarified that these stocks accounted for less than 10% of the portfolio and that the fund house was not taking an excessively large exposure to the sector.Responding to the argument that AI could make traditional software services businesses obsolete, he said market narratives often become exaggerated and can create investment opportunities.Commenting on why PPFAS Mutual Fund is selective about mid-cap and small-cap stocks, Thakkar said the fund house does not have anything against small-cap or mid-cap stocks and would invest in them when valuations become attractive. However, it would remain selective rather than buying companies simply because they belong to a particular market-cap segment or are part of a popular theme.He pointed out that several companies held by the fund house, including REITs and natural gas businesses, fall within the mid-cap space. He added that small-cap returns can look very attractive when investors enter at the right time, but can be disappointing during other market cycles. He also noted that the small-cap premium has been declining globally..Addressing another frequently discussed concern among unitholders, Thakkar shared his views on whether a mutual fund's size affects its ability to generate returns.He said he had used several AI tools to examine the relationship between fund size and performance across different mutual fund categories. The impact of size is more relevant in the small-cap category.He also highlighted the importance of expense ratios, pointing out that larger funds typically have lower expense ratios, which can benefit investors. articles.title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
articles.text:
At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo
articles.text:
If you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge.

Tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES. He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too.

It’s not a big model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model.

There are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference.

Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an issue given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB.

Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all.

“It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.”

If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above.

If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge.

“The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.”

That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun.

“ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edwards told us.

While a human may have designed the experiment, the coding work was done by AI, Edwards told us – he’s been interested in it since the 1990s and is pursuing more experiments with tiny AI models using the help of the bigger ones.

“I've been theorizing about what I call ‘tiny talking machines’ … over the past year,” Edwards told us, and he’s been able to use coding agents to turn those ideas into actual software. ChatGPT for SNES is one example, and he also created an NES ROM called Séance that uses an even smaller AI model able to run on an original Nintendo Entertainment System that simulates talking to a ghost in a haunted game cartridge.

“I designed the scope of what the software should be, how it should work broadly, what chip it should use, how the interface should look and work, and the sounds it makes when it types responses,” Edwards told us. He added that he sees the project as an AI/human collaboration, which is where he believes AI works best.

“The AI agents who did the coding for this project currently advise that we've hit the limit of how good the AI model can be on the limited hardware,” Edwards said - he’s not taking their word for it, though. “It's up to human creativity to transcend those assumptions. I have already come up with new ideas that I believe can make a tiny model like ChatGPT for SNES even more coherent, and I'm working on them now.” ®
