From record highs to a brutal rout: What is behind the meltdown in gold and silver?
articles.text: Gold and silver are witnessing a sharp reversal after their spectacular rally, with a strengthening US dollar, increasingly hawkish Federal Reserve expectations and investor liquidations triggering a sustained sell-off across precious metals.The correction has been particularly severe in silver, which has plunged 41% over the past six months, compared with a 19% decline in gold. The selling has accelerated over the past month, with silver losing 19% and gold falling 9%.Spot gold was quoted at $3,524.80 an ounce, down 4.33%, while spot silver traded at $40.99 an ounce, declining around 7%.Why are gold and silver falling?A major trigger for gold's latest decline has been the changing outlook for US monetary policy, with increasingly hawkish signals from Federal Reserve policymakers strengthening expectations of further interest-rate increases.According to Reuters, comments from US Federal Reserve policymakers have reinforced the hawkish tone of the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson flagged inflation risks that could warrant another interest-rate increase, strengthening expectations that US borrowing costs could rise further.Markets are pricing in a 96% probability of a 25-basis-point US rate hike in December, according to the CME FedWatch tool.Minutes of the Fed's October 27-28 meeting, released on Wednesday, also highlighted spolicymakers' concerns about persistent inflation pressures. Although the central bank left interest rates unchanged, some participants supported a 25-basis-point increase at the October meeting, while a couple flagged the possibility of a larger increase in December.Artificial intelligence-related demand also featured in the discussions, with policymakers identifying it as a material source of inflation risk.The changing interest-rate outlook has strengthened the US dollar, which has climbed to a 19-month high. A stronger dollar makes dollar-denominated bullion more expensive for buyers using other currencies, adding to the pressure on prices.Higher interest rates also increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which does not generate interest income, making yield-bearing assets relatively more attractive.Gold struggles to find safe-haven supportThe latest decline has come despite renewed tensions in the Middle East. Even as gold has entered increasingly oversold territory, bullion has struggled to attract buying, with the dollar's strength, rising yield expectations and investor liquidations outweighing its traditional safe-haven appeal.On Friday, gold fell to $3,513.54 an ounce, its lowest level since September 4, 2025.Bullion had lost around 8% during the week, putting it on course for its steepest weekly decline in eight months. US gold futures for December delivery fell 2.7% to $3,587.90 an ounce.The ongoing sell-off in artificial intelligence-related equities has also contributed to the pressure, with some investors reportedly liquidating gold positions to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios.Tony Sage, CEO of Critical Metals, said gold was under renewed pressure from hawkish Federal Reserve expectations, which were lifting real yields and the US dollar while increasing the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset."The ongoing AI-related equity selloff is also prompting some forced liquidations of gold positions to cover losses elsewhere," Sage said.Why has silver fallen more sharply than gold?Silver's 41% decline over six months, against gold's 19% fall, highlights the greater volatility of the white metal.According to Sage, silver, platinum and palladium are declining alongside gold primarily because of the same macroeconomic drivers. However, silver's typically higher volatility has amplified the market movement."Silver, platinum and palladium are declining in tandem with gold primarily because of the same macro drivers. Silver is typically more volatile and has amplified the move this week," Sage said.He added that platinum and palladium were also sensitive to growth concerns accompanying tighter monetary policy.Investment demand remains an important supportThe accumulation strategy comes even as the World Gold Council expects investment demand to remain the leading driver of growth in gold demand in 2026.However, the council has lowered its forecast for the increase in average annual gold demand from 400 tonnes to 200 tonnes year-on-year.Gold ETF inflows have exceeded expectations, while demand for bars and coins has remained relatively resilient, although it slowed considerably in the second half of the year.ETF inflows during the third quarter were particularly notable, coming despite a sharp rise in bond yields, a stronger US dollar and a decline in the Geopolitical Risk Index.The data suggests that concerns around fiscal conditions and broader economic uncertainty have partly offset the higher opportunity cost of holding gold.Gold finds support at $3,500; silver at $38-$39Anindya Banerjee, Head of Commodity, Currency and Rate Derivatives at Kotak Neo, said $3,500 remains the first important support level for gold, within a broader support zone of $3,400-$3,500."We would look for a daily hammer or doji in that area, followed by buying in the next session. That would be the first evidence that the market is absorbing the selling. Until then, the trend remains down," Banerjee said.For silver, the next major support zone is seen at $38-$39 an ounce. Banerjee said the metal would also need a similar reversal signal to indicate that selling pressure was easing.The next move in precious metals will depend on the interplay between US monetary policy, currency movements and global demand. articles.title: NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches
articles.text:
It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week.

For Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications issue that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission.

The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century.

In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters.

Earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain.

More bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt.

In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth.

The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode.

So far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output.

Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the issues – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold.

Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®
